name: Clausius’s heat-work reconciliation
summary: Clausius showed that an engine turns part of its heat into work while the rest flows from hot to cold, reconciling Carnot's theory with heat–work equivalence.
description: Clausius combined equivalence of heat and work with a modified Carnot argument: part of the heat can be converted to work while another part passes from a warmer body to a colder one.
tier_reason: Reconciliation of heat/work and reversible engines supplies a reusable foundation for thermodynamics and later physical theory.
why: Evidence that heat and work are equivalent clashed with Carnot's argument as originally framed, and Clausius modified the argument so both could stand.

market.note: Commercial availability is not a milestone of a scientific knowledge result.

date.label: 1850; publication month unresolved
date.basis: The 1867 editorial note reports March–April 1850, while Thomson in 1851 dates the second-part proof to May 1850. The year is supported; the conflicting month reports are preserved.

events.statement: Clausius’s memoir was published in 1850; inspected sources disagree on the publication month of its second part.
events.caveats: The 1867 English collection reports March–April publication; Thomson 1851 §14 reports May publication of the second-part proof. The original journal issues have not resolved the disagreement. Berlin is established for the February communication, not the publication location.

evidence.locator: First Memoir, printed pp. 14–18 and 68–69; p. 14 visually checked
evidence.supports: 1850 communication, mediated Carnot access, explicit Joule evidence, response to Thomson and proposed reconciliation.

date.label: 1852 publication
date.basis: Thomson’s detailed printed credit or use appears in the Philosophical Magazine volume for July–December 1852. A 1851 reading is not treated as proof of the exact contents of that oral presentation.

events.statement: Thomson explicitly credited Clausius for establishing the reversible-engine proposition on revised principles and compared their arguments in the 1852 printed paper.
events.scope: Clausius’s combination of heat–work equivalence with a modified reversible-engine proposition.
events.caveats: Thomson says his own proof was independently developed. The 1851 paper was read to the Edinburgh society, but the exact wording present in that oral presentation is not independently established.

evidence.supports: The 1852 original journal printing explicitly contains the stated credit or numerical use.

links.statement: Clausius stated that he knew Carnot’s work through Clapeyron and Thomson, and identified Clapeyron’s analytical treatment as a source for the 1850 investigation.
links.scope: First Memoir, opening and first footnotes.
links.alternatives: Thomson supplied another explicit channel; Joule’s experiments supplied a distinct empirical input.
links.caveats: No direct Carnot-to-Clausius reading edge is asserted for 1850.
links.timing: 1834/1837 text precedes 1850 use; the later 1864 statement of direct access is excluded.

evidence.locator: Printed p. 14, main text and Carnot/Clapeyron footnotes
evidence.supports: Direct statement of mediated reading; original 1850 portion distinguished from bracketed 1864 addition.

links.statement: Clausius invoked Joule’s experiments as evidence for heat production proportional to work, and specifically compared the earlier magneto-electric equivalent with his theory.
links.scope: 1850 First Memoir, opening argument and numerical comparison.
links.alternatives: Gas and later friction experiments are also named; no single measurement uniquely establishes the full theory.
links.caveats: The source uses converted historical units; this relationship does not silently equate all reference-temperature conventions.
links.timing: 1843 result precedes 1850 discussion; no uncertain dependence on the publication timing of the 1850 Joule paper is needed.

evidence.locator: Printed p. 15 and p. 68, footnote to Philosophical Magazine XXIII p. 441
evidence.supports: Experimental justification and specific reference to Joule’s 1843 numerical result.

links.statement: Clausius explicitly answered Thomson’s provisional defense of Carnot’s theory, proposing that heat consumption and transfer could occur together.
links.scope: Clausius’s 1850 opening discussion of Thomson’s 1849 account.
links.alternatives: Clapeyron, Holtzmann and Joule are additional named inputs.
links.caveats: An explicit critical response, not a claim that Thomson already held Clausius’s solution.

evidence.supports: Identifies Thomson’s use of Regnault and Joule, quotes his difficulty, and responds with the reconciliation.

links.statement: Clausius used Regnault’s steam measurements in the numerical evaluation of his heat-work argument.
links.scope: Only the identified configurations and source-described contribution.
links.alternatives: No unique historical route or universal necessity asserted.
links.caveats: This is a particular numerical input, not a claim that Regnault supplied the whole theory.
links.timing: The 1847 published data precede Clausius’s 1850 memoir; publication month remains unresolved.

evidence.supports: Explicit attribution and numerical use of Regnault’s latent-heat results.
